name: Rayleigh Scattering
statement: Small particles scatter short blue light far more than long red light, so the sky is blue.
meaning: Rayleigh scattering is the scattering of light by particles much smaller than its wavelength, such as the molecules of the air. Its defining feature is a steep dependence on wavelength: the scattered intensity is inversely proportional to the fourth power of the wavelength, so short-wavelength blue light is scattered far more strongly than long-wavelength red. This is why the daytime sky is blue and why the Sun reddens near the horizon.
mechanism: The oscillating electric field of the light drives the charges in a small molecule or particle to oscillate, turning it into a tiny radiating dipole that re-emits light in new directions. Because the strength of this re-radiation rises sharply as wavelength shrinks, the intensity scales with one over the fourth power of the wavelength: halving the wavelength scatters sixteen times as much. So blue is scattered out of a sunbeam much more than red, painting the sky blue with scattered blue light and leaving the transmitted beam reddened over a long path.

examples.text: Air molecules scatter blue sunlight in all directions far more than red, filling the daytime sky with blue light.
Near the horizon sunlight travels a long path through the atmosphere, scattering away most of the blue and leaving the direct light orange to red.
Cloud droplets are comparable to or larger than the wavelength, so they scatter all colours nearly equally by Mie scattering, which is why clouds look white, not blue.

variants.name: Mie scattering
variants.text: The regime for particles comparable to or larger than the wavelength, where scattering is nearly wavelength-independent and whitish, governing clouds, fog, and mist rather than the clear sky.

variants.name: The Tyndall effect
variants.text: The earlier observation, by John Tyndall, of bluish scattering from fine particles in a medium, a forerunner of Rayleigh's quantitative treatment.

whyItMatters: It explains one of the most familiar facts about the world, the colour of the sky and of sunsets, and it underpins how light propagates through the atmosphere and other clear media. It matters for astronomy, remote sensing, and optics, sets a floor on losses in optical fibres, and provides the textbook contrast with Mie scattering that separates the blue sky from the white cloud.

working.text: apply Rayleigh scattering when scatterers are much smaller than the wavelength; for larger particles use Mie scattering instead.
remember that shorter wavelengths scatter far more, with intensity rising as one over the fourth power of wavelength.
look to scattered light for the blue sky and to the long-path transmitted beam for the red sunset.

limits: It is valid only when the scattering particles are much smaller than the wavelength of light, as air molecules are; for particles comparable to or larger than the wavelength the fourth-power law fails and Mie scattering, nearly independent of colour, takes over. It idealises the scatterers as small dipoles and does not by itself capture multiple scattering, absorption, or the full three-factor account of sky colour, which also involves the Sun's spectrum and the response of the eye.
misreadings: The sky is not blue because it reflects the ocean; the colour comes from atmospheric scattering and appears even far inland. The sky is not violet, even though violet scatters still more, because sunlight contains less violet and the eye is far less sensitive to it, so the mix reads as blue. And Rayleigh scattering is not what makes clouds white: that is Mie scattering by larger droplets, nearly the same for every colour.
origin: Named after the British physicist Lord Rayleigh (John William Strutt), who quantified the effect in an 1871 paper and later, by 1899, showed it applied to the air's own molecules; it built on John Tyndall's earlier observations.
